content: The study involved six occupational therapists (OTs), one physical therapy assistant, and one OT assistant. Clinicians primarily gained knowledge about manual wheelchair (MWC) training through informal mentorship from experienced colleagues or trial-and-error methods, rather than relying on validated, research-based resources. Few clinicians were aware of or utilized validated MWC training resources, such as Clinical Practice Guidelines (CPGs) or the Wheelchair Skills Training Program (WSTP). A training program for medical students included a 4-hour workshop with didactic, practical, community, and reflective components. This intervention improved students' knowledge and skills related to wheelchair use, although it did not significantly change their attitudes. Qualitative evidence suggested a positive impact on their understanding of wheelchair users' needs. Occupational therapy students participated in simulation-based training across seven clinical scenarios, which included video demonstrations, peer practice, and performance assessments. This approach effectively taught wheelchair transfer techniques, handling skills, and clinical reasoning. Students also reviewed digital videos of their performance to improve their skills. A two-day wheelchair skills boot camp for final-year occupational therapy students, based on the Wheelchair Skills Program, enhanced their ability to assess, train, and document manual and power wheelchair skills. This training approach was deemed practical and effective for integrating wheelchair skills education into time-intensive curricula. A study in Colombia assessed the basic wheelchair provision knowledge of final-year OT students using the ISWP Wheelchair Service Provision Basic Knowledge Test. None of the students achieved the minimum passing score of 70%, indicating significant gaps in their education. The findings highlighted that current wheelchair provision education in OT programs does not meet WHO guidelines. A qualitative study described the integration of wheelchair service provision education into rehabilitation programs. It emphasized the importance of context-specific training to meet the needs of wheelchair users. Students expressed the value of wheelchair-specific courses in their professional training and recommended incorporating such training into OT curricula. The Wheelchair Skills Training Program (WSTP) for caregivers demonstrated improvements in their wheelchair-handling skills. Training was individualized, with immediate feedback provided when skills were not performed safely or effectively. The program was found to be safe, practical, and effective, with skills generally retained and transferable to community settings. A cross-sectional study revealed that health professionals were most confident in teaching wheelchair transfers (93%), activities of daily living (ADLs, 81%), and basic mobility (80%). However, confidence was lower for advanced mobility (35%) and maintenance/repair (52%). Additional training was desired, particularly for advanced skills and outdoor mobility. A narrative review highlighted the lack of assistive technology education in professional therapy degrees, leading to inexperienced therapists assisting consumers. This gap contributes to technology abandonment, wasted funding, and delays in providing necessary equipment. Continuing education and pre-service training in assistive technology are essential to address these issues. A randomized controlled trial found that a 2-hour educational wheelchair program, including interactive experiences, improved medical students' comfort in managing wheelchair users. Most participants reported increased understanding and confidence in treating patients who use wheelchairs. Overall, these findings underscore the need for comprehensive, validated, and context-specific wheelchair skills training across medical and rehabilitation education programs to improve service delivery and meet the needs of wheelchair users effectively.
